items.topic: Regulations governing practice before the IRS (Circular 230)
items.task: Identify who may practice before the IRS and the scope of that practice.
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: Which of the following persons does NOT have unlimited authority to represent a taxpayer before every function of the IRS, including Appeals and Collection?
options: A paid preparer whose only credential is a PTIN and an Annual Filing Season Program Record of Completion
An enrolled agent who has passed all three parts of the Special Enrollment Examination and holds a current enrollment card
A CPA in good standing with the licensing authority of a state
An attorney in good standing before the highest court of a state

why.A: Holders of that record have only limited representation rights, and only for returns they prepared and signed. Unlimited rights belong to attorneys, CPAs and enrolled agents; enrolled actuaries and enrolled retirement plan agents may practice only on the specific matters listed in Circular 230 section 10.3(d)(2) and (e)(2).
why.B: Enrolled agents are enrolled to practice and have unlimited representation rights before all IRS offices.
why.C: A CPA in good standing may practice before the IRS without further enrollment and has unlimited rights.
why.D: An attorney in good standing has unlimited practice rights; no IRS enrollment is required.

items.law_note: Post-Loving v. IRS (2014) structure; the RTRP designation is no longer valid.
items.rule_line: Only attorneys, CPAs and enrolled agents have unlimited IRS practice rights; enrolled actuaries and retirement plan agents may practice only on the matters listed in Circular 230; a Record of Completion gives limited rights only.

guide.ask: Which credentials carry unlimited representation rights before every IRS function?
guide.reveal: Attorneys, CPAs and enrolled agents.

guide.ask: What can a holder of only a PTIN and an Annual Filing Season Program Record of Completion do?
guide.reveal: Limited representation only, and only for returns that person prepared and signed.

items.topic: Regulations governing practice before the IRS (Circular 230)
items.task: Identify who may practice before the IRS and the scope of that practice.
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: Mira Kowalski holds a PTIN but no CPA, attorney or enrolled agent credential and no Annual Filing Season Program Record of Completion. In 2026 she prepared and signed a client's 2025 Form 1040. The IRS now opens an examination of that return. May Mira represent the client before the revenue agent?
options: Yes, but only before revenue agents, since she prepared and signed the return
Yes, in any IRS matter, if the client signs a power of attorney naming her
Yes, because she is compensated to prepare the return and is therefore a tax return preparer
No, because she has no credential or Record of Completion giving representation rights

why.A: This was the rule for returns prepared and signed before 2016. It no longer applies to a preparer with no credential and no Record of Completion.
why.B: A power of attorney only names a representative; it does not give authority to a person who is not eligible to practice.
why.C: Being a paid preparer creates preparer duties and penalties. It does not give the right to represent a taxpayer.
why.D: For returns prepared and signed after 2015, an unenrolled preparer without a credential or Record of Completion has no right to represent the taxpayer in an examination.

items.rule_line: A preparer with no credential and no Record of Completion cannot represent a client in an examination of a return prepared after 2015.

guide.ask: Which credentials or record give a preparer the right to represent a client in an examination?
guide.reveal: CPA, attorney, enrolled agent, or an Annual Filing Season Program Record of Completion.

guide.ask: Does Mira hold any of these?
guide.reveal: No, she holds only a PTIN, so she has no representation rights in the exam.

items.topic: Regulations governing practice before the IRS (Circular 230)
items.task: Identify who may practice before the IRS and the scope of that practice.
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: A client signs Form 8821, Tax Information Authorization, naming her CPA. What may the CPA do under that form?
options: Receive the client's tax information, but not represent the client or sign for her
Represent the client at a Collection Appeals hearing and sign a closing agreement for her
Sign the client's amended return and endorse the resulting refund check
Tell the IRS what settlement amount the client would accept in an examination

why.A: Form 8821 authorizes access to tax information only. Representation before the IRS requires a power of attorney on Form 2848.
why.B: Representing a taxpayer and signing agreements require Form 2848, not Form 8821.
why.C: A preparer signs only as preparer. Endorsing or negotiating a client's refund check is prohibited by Circular 230.
why.D: Negotiating a settlement is representation, which requires Form 2848.

items.rule_line: Form 8821 authorizes receipt of tax information only; representation requires Form 2848 power of attorney.

guide.ask: What does Form 8821 authorize compared with Form 2848?
guide.reveal: Form 8821 lets the named person receive tax information; Form 2848 is the power of attorney for representation.

guide.ask: Given that, which actions can the CPA take on Form 8821 alone?
guide.reveal: Receive information only, with no representing, signing or negotiating for the client.

items.topic: Regulations governing practice before the IRS (Circular 230)
items.task: Identify who may practice before the IRS and the scope of that practice.
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: Circular 230 lets certain persons represent others before the IRS without being an attorney, CPA or enrolled agent. In which situation is the representative NOT covered by such an exception?
options: A full-time employee represents his employer in an IRS matter
A general partner represents her partnership before the IRS
A taxpayer's adult child represents the taxpayer, her parent, at the IRS
An unpaid friend with no credential and no family tie represents the taxpayer

why.A: A regular full-time employee may represent his employer, so this is permitted.
why.B: A general partner may represent the partnership; this is a listed exception.
why.C: An individual may represent a member of his or her immediate family without enrolling.
why.D: Friendship is not a listed relationship. The exceptions cover the taxpayer herself and specified relationships such as family, corporate officers, partners and fiduciaries.

items.rule_line: Circular 230 exceptions cover the taxpayer, family, employees, partners, officers and fiduciaries, not an unrelated friend.

guide.ask: Which relationships let a non-credentialed person represent a taxpayer under Circular 230?
guide.reveal: The taxpayer personally, family members, corporate officers or employees, partners and fiduciaries.

guide.ask: Is friendship on that list?
guide.reveal: No, so an unpaid friend with no tie is not covered.

items.topic: Regulations governing practice before the IRS (Circular 230)
items.task: Apply a practitioner's duties, restrictions and standards under Circular 230 to a scenario.
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: During work on a client's 2025 return, Hana Cho, CPA, learns that the client omitted $30,000 of income from the 2023 return Hana's firm prepared. What must Hana do under Circular 230?
options: Promptly advise the client of the omission and its consequences
Report the omission to the IRS within 30 days
Amend the 2023 return without informing the client because the firm prepared it
Resign from the engagement and notify the client's lender of the reason

why.A: A practitioner who knows of a client's error or omission must advise the client of it and its consequences. Circular 230 does not require reporting it to the IRS.
why.B: Circular 230 does not require the practitioner to disclose the error to the IRS, and return information generally cannot be disclosed without consent.
why.C: A practitioner cannot amend a return without the client's knowledge and signature.
why.D: Resigning is not required, and telling a third party would breach confidentiality.

items.rule_line: A practitioner who knows of a client's return error must advise the client of the error and consequences, but need not report it to the IRS.

guide.ask: What does Circular 230 require of a practitioner who knows of a client's omission?
guide.reveal: Advise the client promptly of the omission and its consequences.

guide.ask: Must the practitioner report it to the IRS or amend the return alone?
guide.reveal: No, the duty is to advise the client, not to report or unilaterally amend.

items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: Rafael Ortiz, CPA, receives a proper written IRS request for records he holds for a client's 2024 return, which is under examination. The records are not privileged, and the client tells Rafael to ignore the request. What must Rafael do?
options: Refuse, because client confidentiality overrides any IRS request for records unless the IRS obtains a summons
Wait until the IRS issues a summons before providing anything
Give the IRS only the records that are favorable to the client
Promptly submit the records, because he has no good-faith basis to claim privilege

why.A: There is no general confidentiality exception to a proper IRS request. Only a good-faith belief that the records are privileged permits refusal.
why.B: A practitioner must not delay a proper informal request by insisting on a summons when no privilege applies.
why.C: Selective production would breach the duty to respond promptly and could itself be sanctionable conduct.
why.D: A practitioner must promptly give the IRS records it properly requests unless he reasonably and in good faith believes they are privileged. The client's instruction is not a basis to refuse.

items.rule_line: A practitioner must promptly submit properly requested IRS records unless in good faith believing them privileged; client instruction is no excuse.

guide.ask: When must a practitioner give the IRS records it properly requests?
guide.reveal: Promptly, unless he reasonably and in good faith believes the records are privileged.

guide.ask: Do these records qualify as privileged, and does the client's instruction change the duty?
guide.reveal: They are not privileged and the client's instruction does not excuse refusal, so Rafael must submit them promptly.

items.stem: Delia Nunez, EA, is asked to accept one of four fee arrangements by a client. Which arrangement is permitted under Circular 230?
options: 25% of any tax reduction, for representing the client in an examination of a filed 2023 return
15% of the refund, for preparing the client's original 2025 return
A fee that the client sets after the work, payable only if the client is satisfied
10% of the tax saved, for advising the client on a proposed position before any return is filed

why.A: A contingent fee is permitted for services connected with an IRS examination of, or challenge to, an original return.
why.B: A contingent fee for preparing an original return is prohibited.
why.C: Outside the permitted categories, a fee may not depend on the outcome of the matter.
why.D: Advice before a return is filed is not an examination or judicial matter, so a contingent fee is not permitted.

items.rule_line: Circular 230 permits contingent fees only for IRS examinations, challenges to original returns and certain refund claims or court matters, not original return preparation.

guide.ask: When is a contingent fee allowed under Circular 230?
guide.reveal: When the services relate to an IRS examination of, or challenge to, an original return.

guide.ask: Which of the four arrangements involves such services?
guide.reveal: The percentage fee for representing the client in an examination of a filed return.

items.stem: Lucas Ferreira, CPA, considers four fee proposals. Which one is permitted under both Circular 230 and the AICPA Code of Professional Conduct?
options: 25% of the refund, for preparing an original return for a non-attest client
20% of the refund, for preparing an amended return for a non-attest client
10% of the tax benefit, for tax planning advice to a client for whom Lucas performs the audit
30% of the tax saved, for representing a non-attest client in an IRS examination

why.A: Both sets of rules prohibit a contingent fee for preparing an original return.
why.B: The AICPA Code prohibits a contingent fee for preparing an amended return, apart from the examination and court exceptions.
why.C: The AICPA Code bars any contingent fee from an attest client, so this fails.
why.D: Both sets of rules allow a contingent fee for representing a client in an examination by a taxing authority.

items.rule_line: Contingent fees for representation in an IRS examination are allowed under both Circular 230 and the AICPA Code for non-attest clients.

guide.ask: Which contingent fees does Circular 230 allow?
guide.reveal: Those tied to representation in an examination or challenge of a return.

guide.ask: Which of those does the AICPA Code also allow for a CPA?
guide.reveal: Representation before a taxing authority in an examination; original-return preparation and fees for an attest client are not allowed.

items.stem: Nora Patel, CPA, prepared a client's 2025 return. The client disputes Nora's $2,000 fee and has not paid it. The client asks for the records she supplied, which the client needs to file the client's federal return. Nora is holding them until she is paid. Which statement is correct?
options: Nora must return the records promptly despite the fee dispute; she may keep copies
Nora may keep the records until the fee is paid in full, because she holds a lien
Nora must return the records only after the client files a formal request with the IRS
Nora must return the records but may first charge a $500 release fee

why.A: A practitioner must return client records on request, and a fee dispute does not excuse holding them when the client needs them to meet tax obligations.
why.B: Circular 230 requires return of the records the client needs to comply with federal tax obligations even when a fee dispute exists; a state-law lien does not let the practitioner hold them as leverage (the Section 10.28(b) exception covers only records already attached to a return or state-law lien rights over other records).
why.C: The client's own request is enough; the IRS is not involved.
why.D: A practitioner may not condition the return of records on payment of a release fee.

items.rule_line: A practitioner must promptly return client records the client needs for tax compliance despite a fee dispute, and may keep copies.

guide.ask: Does a fee dispute let a practitioner keep client records the client needs?
guide.reveal: No, a practitioner must return client records on request when the client needs them for tax obligations.

guide.ask: May the practitioner keep anything?
guide.reveal: Copies only; the records themselves go back promptly.

items.stem: Priya Shah's CPA firm represents Kim Yoon in an IRS examination. The firm also represents Kim's former partner Lee Grant, whose examination requires Lee to take a position directly adverse to Kim. What is required for the firm to continue with both clients?
options: Only Kim's oral consent, given at the start of the engagement, since Kim is the earlier client and Lee's matter arose later
No consent is needed, because both matters are before the same IRS office and involve the same tax years
Each client gives informed written consent within 30 days, and the firm reasonably believes it can serve both
Written consent from the IRS examiner assigned to both cases

why.A: Consent must come from every affected client, and it must be in writing.
why.B: Representing directly adverse interests creates a conflict regardless of the office.
why.C: A conflict may be waived only if the practitioner reasonably believes he can provide competent, diligent representation and each affected client gives informed written consent within 30 days of learning of the conflict.
why.D: The waiver comes from the clients, not from the IRS.

items.rule_line: Directly adverse client conflicts are waivable only if the practitioner reasonably believes he can serve both and each client gives informed written consent within 30 days.

guide.ask: What conflict standard must the firm meet to continue with directly adverse clients?
guide.reveal: It must reasonably believe it can provide competent and diligent representation to each.

guide.ask: What consent is required and by when?
guide.reveal: Informed written consent from each affected client within 30 days of learning of the conflict.

items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: Which of the following is prohibited by Circular 230?
options: A practitioner asks that a client's refund be deposited directly into the client's own bank account
A practitioner accepts a client's check payable to the firm for tax preparation fees
A practitioner returns a client's refund check to the client by certified mail
A practitioner endorses a client's Treasury refund check and deposits it in the firm's account

why.A: Direct deposit to the client's own account is proper; the practitioner does not handle the funds.
why.B: The prohibition covers government checks issued to the client, not payments the client makes for fees.
why.C: Delivering the check to the client is not endorsing or negotiating it.
why.D: A practitioner may not endorse or negotiate a check issued to a client by the government for a federal tax liability.

items.rule_line: A practitioner may not endorse or negotiate a Treasury refund check issued to a client.

guide.ask: What may a practitioner do with a Treasury refund check issued to a client?
guide.reveal: Nothing that negotiates it; the check must go to the client.

guide.ask: Which action would endorse or negotiate the check?
guide.reveal: Endorsing it and depositing it in the firm's account.

items.task: Apply a practitioner's duties, restrictions and standards under Circular 230 to a scenario.
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: Jonas Weiss prepares the Schedule C for a client. The client provides $45,000 of meals expenses on gross receipts of $60,000 and offers no explanation. Under Circular 230, what is Jonas's duty?
options: He may rely on the information in good faith, but must inquire because it looks incomplete
He must audit all of the client's records before preparing the return
He may accept the figures as given, since the client is responsible for the return's contents
He must refuse the engagement and report the client to the IRS

why.A: A practitioner may rely without independent verification but may not ignore the implications of information he knows, and must inquire when it looks incorrect, inconsistent or incomplete.
why.B: There is no duty to audit or verify client information in every case.
why.C: Good-faith reliance is not available when the information is inconsistent on its face; inquiry is required.
why.D: Nothing requires refusal or reporting; the required step is to inquire.

items.rule_line: A practitioner may rely in good faith on client information but must inquire when it appears incorrect, inconsistent or incomplete.

guide.ask: May a practitioner rely on client information without verification?
guide.reveal: Yes in good faith, but he may not ignore what he knows.

guide.ask: What must he do when meals of $45,000 on $60,000 of receipts looks off?
guide.reveal: Make reasonable inquiries because the information looks inconsistent or incomplete.

items.task: Apply a practitioner's duties, restrictions and standards under Circular 230 to a scenario.

items.stem: Owen Blake, CPA, is preparing a return that includes a deduction with a reasonable basis but without substantial authority. No reportable transaction is involved and Owen is not acting willfully. Which action satisfies Circular 230 as to that position?
options: Sign the return after the position is adequately disclosed on it
Sign the return without disclosure, since reasonable basis alone is enough
Sign the return without disclosure and tell the client to expect a penalty
Sign the return if the client agrees to pay any resulting penalty

why.A: A position that lacks substantial authority but has a reasonable basis may be signed if it is adequately disclosed.
why.B: Without disclosure the position is unreasonable because it lacks substantial authority.
why.C: Informing the client does not cure a position that is unreasonable when undisclosed.
why.D: A client's promise to pay is not a substitute for the disclosure or authority required.

items.rule_line: A position with reasonable basis but without substantial authority may be signed only if adequately disclosed on the return.

guide.ask: What authority level does the position have?
guide.reveal: Reasonable basis but not substantial authority.

guide.ask: What must happen before a preparer signs a position with only reasonable basis?
guide.reveal: It must be adequately disclosed on the return.

items.task: Apply a practitioner's duties, restrictions and standards under Circular 230 to a scenario.
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: Kai Nakamura, CPA, advises a client about an aggressive return position that could draw a penalty. Under Circular 230, what must Kai tell the client?
options: Nothing, if the client has signed an engagement letter accepting the risk
The penalties that may apply and how disclosure can avoid them
Only the interest that would accrue, because penalties are the IRS's concern
That the position may not be taken unless the client obtains a written tax opinion

why.A: An engagement letter does not remove the duty to inform.
why.B: A practitioner must advise a client of potentially applicable penalties and of the opportunity to avoid them through disclosure, and explain the disclosure requirements.
why.C: The duty specifically covers penalties, not just interest.
why.D: Circular 230 does not require an opinion for every aggressive position.

items.rule_line: A practitioner must advise a client of potential penalties on a position and how adequate disclosure can avoid them.

guide.ask: What must a practitioner tell a client about an aggressive position?
guide.reveal: The potential penalties that may apply.

guide.ask: What else must be explained?
guide.reveal: The opportunity to avoid penalties through disclosure and the disclosure requirements.

items.task: Apply a practitioner's duties, restrictions and standards under Circular 230 to a scenario.
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: Which of the following is prohibited when a practitioner gives written tax advice under Circular 230?
options: Making a reasonable factual assumption and stating it in the advice
Relying on a client representation that the practitioner has reason to believe is reasonable
Assuming the return will not be audited or the issue will not be raised
Considering all relevant facts that the practitioner knows

why.A: Reasonable assumptions may be used if they are identified and supported.
why.B: Reasonable reliance on representations is allowed.
why.C: A practitioner may not take into account the possibility that a return will not be audited or that an issue will not be raised.
why.D: Considering all relevant facts is a requirement, not a prohibition.

items.rule_line: Written tax advice may not take into account the possibility that a return will not be audited or an issue not raised.

guide.ask: May a practitioner rely on facts he has reason to believe are reasonable and state assumptions openly?
guide.reveal: Yes, reasonable factual assumptions and reasonable reliance are permitted.

guide.ask: Which consideration is forbidden in written advice?
guide.reveal: Assuming the return will not be audited or the issue will not be raised.

items.task: Apply a practitioner's duties, restrictions and standards under Circular 230 to a scenario.
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: Elena Rossi is the managing partner of a CPA firm. She knows that several staff members routinely sign returns with unsupported positions. The firm has no review procedures and Elena has taken no steps to change that. What is Elena's exposure under Circular 230?
options: None, because only the staff members who signed the returns are responsible
None, unless the IRS first assesses a penalty against a client
Only a civil penalty under the return preparer rules, since Circular 230 discipline applies to the individual signers
She may be sanctioned for not taking reasonable steps to ensure firm-wide compliance procedures

why.A: Circular 230 places responsibility on those with principal authority as well.
why.B: Sanctions do not depend on a client penalty.
why.C: Both regimes can apply; the firm-level duty is set by Circular 230.
why.D: A practitioner with principal authority over a firm's practice must take reasonable steps to ensure adequate compliance procedures, and may be sanctioned when the firm shows a pattern of noncompliance.

items.rule_line: A practitioner with principal authority over a firm must take reasonable steps to ensure firm-wide compliance procedures or face Circular 230 sanction.

guide.ask: What duty does a person with principal authority over a firm's practice have?
guide.reveal: Take reasonable steps to ensure the firm has adequate compliance procedures.

guide.ask: What happens when a firm shows a pattern of noncompliance and no procedures exist?
guide.reveal: That person may be sanctioned, so Elena is exposed.

items.stem: A practitioner who publishes a fee for routine services must, according to Circular 230, adhere to that fee for at least how long after the last date of publication?
options: 7 calendar days
30 calendar days
60 calendar days
90 calendar days

why.A: This is too short; the rule uses a 30-day period.
why.B: A practitioner who publishes fee information must adhere to the published fee for at least 30 calendar days after the last date of publication.
why.C: This is longer than the rule requires.
why.D: This is longer than the rule requires.

items.author_note: 확신 낮음: 30일 기간 조문 원문 재확인 필요
items.rule_line: A practitioner who publishes fees must adhere to them for at least 30 calendar days after the last publication date.

guide.ask: What does Circular 230 say about published fees for routine services?
guide.reveal: The practitioner must adhere to the published fee for a minimum period after last publication.

guide.ask: How long is that period?
guide.reveal: 30 calendar days.

items.topic: Internal Revenue Code and regulations related to tax return preparers
items.task: Identify penalties, requirements and prohibitions that apply to tax return preparers.
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: Dana Whitfield, a paid preparer, prepared a return for a fee of $3,400. The position she took lacked substantial authority and was not disclosed, and Dana cannot show reasonable cause and good faith. She did not act willfully or recklessly. What is Dana's penalty for the unreasonable position?

why.A: Uses the $1,000 floor without checking the 50% alternative, which is larger here.
why.B: The penalty is the greater of $1,000 or 50% of the income derived from the return: 50% x $3,400 = $1,700, which is greater than $1,000.
why.C: Applies the 75% rate for willful or reckless conduct, which is not present.
why.D: Uses the $5,000 floor for willful or reckless conduct.

steps: Unreasonable position, no willfulness: greater of $1,000 or 50% of income derived
items.rule_line: Preparer penalty for an unreasonable position is the greater of $1,000 or 50% of the income derived from the return.

guide.ask: Which preparer penalty applies to an unreasonable position without willfulness?
guide.reveal: Greater of $1,000 or 50% of income derived from the return.

guide.ask: What is 50% of the $3,400 fee?
Which amount is larger?
guide.reveal: 1,700 exceeds 1,000, so the penalty is 1,700.

items.topic: Internal Revenue Code and regulations related to tax return preparers
items.task: Identify penalties, requirements and prohibitions that apply to tax return preparers.
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: A preparer earned $9,200 on a return. The IRS establishes that the preparer willfully understated the client's tax by disregarding the client's documents. Assuming only the willful-or-reckless preparer penalty is asserted, what is the penalty?

why.A: Uses 50%, the rate for an unreasonable position, not willful conduct.
why.B: Uses only the $5,000 floor; 75% of the income is larger.
why.C: For willful or reckless conduct the penalty is the greater of $5,000 or 75% of the income derived: 75% x $9,200 = $6,900.
why.D: Takes the whole fee. The penalty is 75% of the fee, not 100%.

steps: Willful or reckless: greater of $5,000 or 75% of income derived
items.rule_line: Preparer penalty for willful or reckless understatement is the greater of $5,000 or 75% of the income derived from the return.

guide.ask: Which preparer penalty applies to willful or reckless understatement?
guide.reveal: Greater of $5,000 or 75% of income derived.

guide.ask: What is 75% of $9,200?
Which is larger?
guide.reveal: 6,900 exceeds 5,000, so the penalty is 6,900.

items.topic: Internal Revenue Code and regulations related to tax return preparers
items.task: Identify penalties, requirements and prohibitions that apply to tax return preparers.
items.task_source: author-drafted from Blueprint topic name (지도.json has no Group A/B/D)
items.stem: Which of the following persons is a tax return preparer who is subject to the preparer penalty provisions?
options: A CPA paid to prepare most of a client's return who does not sign it
A clerical assistant who only types and copies a return prepared by others
An employee who prepares the employer's own return
A volunteer at a free clinic who prepares a return without compensation

why.A: A nonsigning preparer who prepares all or a substantial portion of a return for compensation is a tax return preparer.
why.B: Merely typing, reproducing or mechanical assistance does not make one a preparer.
why.C: Preparing the employer's own return, without being paid as a preparer, does not make one a preparer.
why.D: The definition requires preparation for compensation.

items.rule_line: A tax return preparer is anyone paid to prepare all or a substantial portion of a return, signing or not.

guide.ask: Who counts as a tax return preparer?
guide.reveal: Anyone who prepares all or a substantial portion of a return for compensation.

guide.ask: Does signing the return matter?

Disclosure is needed only for positions that have substantial authority

why.B: Counts only the failure-to-file addition net of the overlap and omits the failure-to-pay addition.

steps: Months late: April 15 to June 29 is 2 months and 14 days, counted as 3 months

items.stem: Carla Nunez filed her 2025 return 20 days late. She has had no penalties in the prior three years, filed all required returns, and paid the tax due. She asks the IRS to waive the failure-to-file addition. Which administrative relief is most likely available?
options: Automatic waiver, because the return was less than 30 days late
No relief is available for a late return, because the penalty is mandatory
First-time abatement, based on her clean three-year history
Relief only through a Tax Court petition

why.A: There is no automatic waiver based on lateness.
why.B: Reasonable cause and first-time abatement are available.
why.C: The IRS may waive certain penalties administratively if the taxpayer had no penalties in the prior three years, filed all required returns, and paid or arranged to pay the tax.
why.D: Administrative relief may be requested from the IRS without a court case.

items.rule_line: First-time penalty abatement is available administratively for taxpayers with a clean three-year history who filed and paid.

guide.ask: What administrative relief exists for a taxpayer with a clean history?
guide.reveal: First-time penalty abatement.

guide.ask: Which of the taxpayer's facts meet its conditions?
guide.reveal: No penalties in the prior three years, all required returns filed, and the tax paid.

items.stem: Gavin Pryce gave his CPA all the facts about a complex transaction. The CPA, who was experienced in that area, advised a return position. Gavin relied in good faith, but the IRS later disallowed the position. What is the effect on an accuracy-related penalty?
options: Gavin has no defense, because a disallowed position carries the penalty
Gavin has a defense only if the CPA is also an attorney
Gavin has a defense only if he verified the CPA's conclusions with a second, independent adviser before filing
Gavin may avoid the penalty; good-faith reliance on a competent, fully informed adviser is reasonable cause

why.A: Reasonable cause and good faith is a defense to the penalty.
why.B: The adviser need not be an attorney.
why.C: A second opinion is not required.
why.D: Reasonable cause can be shown when the taxpayer gave the adviser complete information, the adviser was competent, and the taxpayer relied in good faith.

items.rule_line: Good-faith reliance on a competent, fully informed adviser can establish reasonable cause and avoid the accuracy-related penalty.

guide.ask: What elements make reliance on an adviser reasonable cause?
guide.reveal: Complete information given, a competent adviser, and good-faith reliance.

guide.ask: Does Gavin meet each element?
guide.reveal: Yes, so he may avoid the penalty even though the position was disallowed.

items.stem: Which of the following carries the highest level of authority for federal tax purposes?
options: The Internal Revenue Code
A Treasury final regulation
A revenue ruling
A Tax Court memorandum decision

why.A: The Code is statute enacted by Congress and outranks regulations, rulings and IRS guidance.
why.B: Regulations interpret the Code and are subordinate to it.
why.C: Revenue rulings are IRS interpretations and rank below regulations.
why.D: A memorandum decision applies to the case decided and is weaker than statute.

items.rule_line: The Internal Revenue Code, as enacted statute, outranks regulations, rulings and court decisions.

guide.ask: What ranks highest among the authorities: statute, regulation, ruling or case?
guide.reveal: Statute enacted by Congress.

guide.ask: What is that source in federal tax law?
guide.reveal: The Internal Revenue Code.

items.stem: Which type of IRS guidance may be relied on as precedent only by the taxpayer to whom it was issued?
options: A revenue ruling
A private letter ruling
A revenue procedure
A final regulation

why.A: Taxpayers with substantially similar facts may rely on a revenue ruling.
why.B: A private letter ruling may not be used or cited as precedent by other taxpayers.
why.C: A revenue procedure states procedural rules that apply to all taxpayers.
why.D: A final regulation binds all taxpayers.

items.rule_line: A private letter ruling may not be cited as precedent by taxpayers other than the one to whom it was issued.

guide.ask: Which IRS guidance is issued to a single taxpayer?
guide.reveal: A private letter ruling.

guide.ask: May other taxpayers cite it as precedent?
guide.reveal: No, only the taxpayer to whom it was issued may rely on it.
